about.projectIntro:
Divrei Dovid is an effort by students, colleagues, and family of Rabbi David Ebner zt"l to gather, preserve, and share his Torah in one accessible home online — the thousands of hours of recorded shiurim and chavrutot, his essays, his poetry, and the marginalia he left in the margins of his own sefarim.

Much of this material has never been made public. It exists in scattered recordings on old hard drives, in a partial archive on Google Drive, and in notebooks and papers still in the possession of his family. Our hope is that his talmidim — and those who never had the chance to learn from him — will be able to find their way back to his voice.

This project is being carried forward by a group of his students, undertaken with the knowledge and support of Rabbi Ebner's family, and in partnership with Yeshivat Eretz Hatzvi. If you have recordings, notes, or materials of his you'd be willing to share — or if you'd like to help organize, transcribe, or support this work — we'd love to hear from you.
about.bioText:
Rabbi David Ebner was born in Bradford, Pennsylvania, in 1945. He received semikha from Yeshiva University, where he studied under Rabbi Joseph B. Soloveitchik, and went on to pursue graduate studies in sociology and Talmud. Before making aliyah, he taught sociology and served as Assistant Director of the Institute for Jewish Life of the United Jewish Communities.

In 1982, Rabbi Ebner and his family moved to Israel, where his life's true calling emerged. For more than two decades he served as Mashgiach Ruchani at Yeshivat HaMivtar in Jerusalem and Efrat, alongside his close friend and partner Rabbi Chaim Brovender. He later helped found Yeshivat Eretz HaTzvi in Jerusalem, where he served as Rosh Yeshiva and spiritual guide. He was also one of the founders of ATID, where he mentored generations of Jewish educators, and he taught for years at ATID–WebYeshiva.org.

Generations of students remember him not only as a teacher of Gemara, but as a rebbe who wove together Halacha, Chassidut, poetry, art, psychology, and literature into what one former talmid called a "Library of Everything." He was as comfortable discussing the Sfas Emes as he was J.D. Salinger, and he taught his students to bring their whole selves — doubts, gifts, and all — into the Beit Midrash. Many describe him as a confidant as much as a teacher: someone who carried their questions and struggles with deep trust and quiet care.

Rabbi Ebner was also a poet, publishing three collections: The Library of Everything, Perhaps This Poem, and Dance Words. His writing, like his teaching, moved fluidly between the sacred and the everyday, reflecting his belief that beauty — in art, music, and language — was itself a doorway to something greater.

Rabbi Ebner passed away in Jerusalem on September 7, 2025, at the age of 80. He is remembered by his family, his many students across the world, and everyone whose life he touched.
about.sourceNote: Bio compiled from Tradition Online, the London School of Jewish Studies, Eretz Hatzvi, ATID, and tributes written by his students. Corrections and additions are welcome — please contact us.
about.graveText:
Rabbi Ebner is buried on the Mount of Olives in Jerusalem. His matzeva (gravestone) describes him as a beloved husband, father, and grandfather — a pillar for his family; the founder and Rosh Yeshiva of Yeshivat Eretz HaTzvi and Mashgiach Ruchani of Yeshivat HaMivtar; a talmid chacham of great depth, a man of many talents, a poet, and a man of spirit, full of grace, wisdom, and knowledge.

It notes that he pursued truth because it was true, that he loved kindness and walked humbly with his G-d, and that he raised many students who illuminate the world with his Torah and his way — and who were to him like sons.

teshuva.intro:
The Dance of Teshuva is a collection of Rav David Ebner zt"l's essays and poetry on the Days of Awe — short pieces, written for reflection in the weeks when a Jew is meant to be doing something about his or her life. They draw on the Torah of Pshischa, Kotzk, Rebbe Nachman, and the Alter of Novardok, with Thoreau and Wordsworth wandering through when they have something to add.

The reader was put together by his students, with a letter of their own introducing it, in the year after his passing.
teshuva.heading: The Dance of Teshuva
teshuva.partnershipText: The Dance of Teshuva is produced and distributed in partnership with 18Forty, the Jewish media and education project led by Rabbi Dovid Bashevkin. When Rav Ebner's students approached 18Forty about collecting his writings into a reader like this one, the team said they jumped at the opportunity — they'd long found that his teachings resonated with the same questions 18Forty tries to explore in its own work. Anonymous donors sponsored the printing and distribution of physical copies in Rav Ebner's memory, so that shuls across the world could have them this holiday season.
teshuva.introEssayHeading: An Introduction, from a Longtime Student
teshuva.introEssayText:
Ahead of Rosh Hashana, Rabbi Mijal Bitton featured the reader in her newsletter, and asked Daniel Bonner — a student of Rav Ebner's for over a decade, first in yeshiva and later weekly over Zoom until his passing — to introduce one of its essays.

Bonner describes him as an “Elul Jew”: most at home in the season of self-examination, open with his students about his own struggles in life, in Torah, and with God. He writes about Rav Ebner's insistence that a real Jewish education has to be lived, not just learned — and about the poet's ear he brought to these Ten Days of Repentance, hearing in them not performance or “fakery,” but what Bonner calls “lived aspiration.”

getInvolved.intro: Divrei Dovid is entirely a labor of love — built and maintained by students who learned from Rabbi Ebner and want his Torah to keep reaching people. There's no single way to help.
getInvolved.heading: Help Carry This Forward
getInvolved.card1Desc: Have a recording, notes, or something he wrote sitting on an old drive? We’d love to add it to the archive.
getInvolved.card2Desc: Volunteer, help organize or transcribe, or help sustain the hosting and printing costs going forward.
getInvolved.card3Desc: If he taught you something you still carry, we’d love for you to share it here.

support.intro: There's no single way to help. Some people have an hour a week to help transcribe or organize. Some are in a position to help sustain the hosting and printing costs going forward. Some just want to say hello. All of it matters — we read every message.
support.heading: Help Carry This Forward

contribute.intro: If you learned with Rabbi Ebner — in a shiur, a chavruta, or a hallway conversation — there's a good chance you're sitting on something we don't have yet: an old cassette, a Zoom recording, typed-up notes, a letter, a poem he wrote you. We'd love to add it to the archive.
contribute.heading: Do You Have a Recording, or Something He Wrote?

tributes.intro: Rabbi Ebner shaped the way thousands of people learn, teach, and think. If he taught you something you still carry — a line, a niggun, a way of asking a question — we'd love for you to share it here: a written memory, a link to something written about him, or a favorite photo of him (or of the two of you). Submissions are lightly reviewed before they're posted.
